title: Holy things
hook: the fifth order: Temple offerings and kosher slaughter

segments.voice: Yesterday, warning the witnesses: one seal, and no two faces alike. Your line was a whole world. Did you stop to ask whether you'd seen it or only heard it? A new week starts today. Day one thousand eighty-six.

One tractate of the Mishnah reads like a builder's notebook. Gates and their names. Chambers and what each was used for. Courtyards, steps, the size of the altar, the places where priests kept watch at night. It's called Middot, measurements. It belongs to the fifth of the Mishnah's six orders, beside tractates on animal offerings, grain offerings, birds, firstborn animals, and what happens when someone uses holy property for themselves. No Temple stands today, and nobody brings these offerings. Yet students still open these pages. Today: the order called holy things.
screen: `A BUILDER'S NOTEBOOK: MIDDOT.` → `OFFERINGS, FIRSTBORN, BIRDS.` → `NO TEMPLE, STILL STUDIED.`

segments.voice: Kodashim. Holy things. In the Mishnah, holiness works like a status. An animal, a measure of flour, a coin: once it's dedicated to the Temple, it is set apart. It doesn't look different. It is different. Turn that idea three ways. First, misuse. A whole tractate, Me'ilah, deals with someone who takes a holy thing and uses it as ordinary property. That's the danger the order guards against: not dirt, but treating the set-apart as if it were just another thing. Second, rhythm. The tractate Tamid describes the daily offering, morning and evening, the Temple's steady heartbeat. One opinion in the Talmud says the daily prayers were set to match those daily offerings. So a Jew praying the morning and afternoon services today is keeping time with a Temple clock. Third, study. With no Temple, what do you do with all these laws? The Talmud gives an answer in the tractate Menachot: whoever studies the law of an offering is counted as if they had brought it. The prophet Hosea had already pictured words offered in place of bulls. So the pages became the altar. People learn the measurements of a building they've never seen, the way you might memorize the layout of a grandparent's house. And there's one more surprise in this order, tucked between the offerings: a tractate about ordinary meat, the kind eaten at home. That's tomorrow. For today, notice the shape of the idea. Something becomes holy when it's set apart, and stays holy as long as it's treated that way.
screen: `HOLINESS AS A STATUS: SET APART.` · `ME'ILAH: DON'T USE IT AS ORDINARY.` · `TAMID: THE TEMPLE'S DAILY CLOCK.` · `STUDY COUNTS AS BRINGING IT.` · then, large: `HOLY THINGS.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: think about what's holy to you. Sit, and let your breath find its own pace. In the Mishnah, a thing becomes holy by being set apart. So look for what you've set apart. An hour of the week. A ring. A letter you keep in a drawer. A walk you only take with one person. A name you don't use lightly. Pick one. Hold it in mind. Then ask the question of Me'ilah: when have I treated it as ordinary? No verdict. Just notice where the line is. The bell holds the time.
Kodashim. Holy things: the Mishnah's fifth order, on the Temple's offerings and what it means for something to be set apart. Today's word.
Your line: holy things. Today, choose one thing you've set apart and treat it that way, on purpose, at least once. Day one thousand eighty-six.

howItsDone: Jews who study Talmud learn the order of Kodashim even though Temple offerings are not brought today, and some traditional prayer books include passages about the offerings in the morning service.
